title: Confucianism: Ritual, Virtue and Relationships
subtitle: Becoming fully human, one bow, one promise, one relationship at a time
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain the core Confucian terms ren, li, junzi, xiao and zhengming in their own context
By the end you will be able to describe how ritual can shape character, using Fingarette's interpretation
By the end you will be able to reconstruct the debate between Mencius and Xunzi on human nature and assess the evidence each used
By the end you will be able to weigh the strongest criticisms of filial piety and of role-based ethics
hook:
Two neighbours meet on the street. One bows slightly and says good morning; the other bows back. Nothing has been exchanged, no information passed, no deal struck. And yet something real has happened: two people have acknowledged each other as people, smoothly and without effort, because they have both learned a shared form.

Most Western moral philosophy you met in this course started elsewhere: with the lone rational chooser deciding what to do (Kant on Day 56), or with the calculation of consequences (Bentham and Mill on Day 61). On Day 87 you briefly met a very different starting point. For **Confucius** (551–479 BCE by traditional dating), morality begins not with a solitary will but with relationships and the shared forms that hold them together: greetings, mourning rites, the way a child serves a parent or a minister advises a ruler. To become good, on this view, is to become skilled at being with others. This lesson takes that idea seriously, with all its power and all its problems.

sections.heading: Master Kong and the Collapse of an Order
sections.body:
The man the Western world calls Confucius was **Kong Qiu**, honoured as **Kongzi** (Master Kong). The Latinised name was popularised by Jesuit missionaries in the seventeenth century. He lived in the small state of Lu, in what is now Shandong province, during the late Spring and Autumn period. The old Zhou dynasty still existed on paper, but real power had splintered among rival lords, and the elaborate ceremonies that once bound the realm together were being usurped, abbreviated or performed cynically.

Kongzi saw himself as a transmitter, not an inventor. He looked back to the founders of the Zhou, especially the Duke of Zhou, as models of rule through virtue. He held minor offices, travelled for years seeking a ruler who would employ him, mostly failed, and spent much of his life teaching. His sayings and conversations were collected by disciples, and by their disciples, into the *Analects* (*Lunyu*, roughly 'Selected Sayings'). Scholars agree the text was compiled over several generations, so it contains layers of different dates. We should speak of 'the Confucius of the *Analects*' rather than pretend we have a transcript.

The *Analects* is not a treatise. It is a collection of short, often enigmatic exchanges. Its most famous self-portrait (2.4) traces a whole life of learning: at fifteen he set his heart on learning, at thirty he took his stand, at forty he had no doubts, and at seventy he could follow his heart's desires without overstepping what was right. Notice the goal. Not a correct theory, but a transformed person whose spontaneous wishes and the demands of morality have become one.

sections.heading: Ren and Li: Humaneness and Ritual Propriety
sections.body:
Two terms carry most of the weight.

**Ren** (仁) is usually translated 'humaneness', 'benevolence' or 'authoritative conduct'. The character combines the signs for 'person' and 'two', and although that etymology is debated, it captures the idea well: ren is the excellence of being human *with* others. When a disciple asked about ren, Kongzi answered simply: love people (12.22). Asked for a single word to guide a whole life, he offered **shu** (恕), reciprocity or 'likening to oneself', and explained it: what you do not want for yourself, do not do to others (15.24). This is sometimes called the 'negative golden rule'.

**Li** (禮) originally meant sacrificial rites to ancestors and spirits. Kongzi widened it to cover the whole fabric of proper conduct: ceremonies, etiquette, the forms of mourning and greeting, the courtesies owed by children to parents and by rulers to subjects. Translators use 'ritual', 'rites' or 'ritual propriety'.

How do the two relate? Kongzi once said that to restrain oneself and return to li is ren (12.1). Yet he also asked: if a person lacks ren, what has he to do with li (3.3)? Scholars disagree about which comes first. One reading: li is the outward form, ren the inner spirit, and each needs the other. Ritual without humaneness is empty theatre; humaneness without ritual is shapeless and clumsy, like a kind person who keeps offending others because they don't know how to express care.

The philosopher **Herbert Fingarette**, in *Confucius: The Secular as Sacred* (1972), gave a famous illustration. When I see you and hold out my hand, you take it without either of us planning or calculating. A handshake is a tiny ritual, and it works as a kind of 'magic': it accomplishes something real (mutual recognition) effortlessly, through shared form. For Fingarette, Kongzi's insight was that human life is full of such ceremonies, and that a good society is one where they are performed sincerely and gracefully.

sections.heading: The Junzi, Rectifying Names and Rule by Virtue
sections.body:
The ideal person in the *Analects* is the **junzi** (君子). The word originally meant 'son of a lord', an aristocrat by birth. Kongzi transformed it into an aristocrat of character, usually translated 'exemplary person' or 'gentleman'. Anyone can become a junzi through learning and self-cultivation; birth is irrelevant. This was a quietly radical idea, and Kongzi reportedly accepted students of humble origin. The junzi is contrasted with the **xiaoren** (小人), the 'small person', who is concerned with profit while the junzi is concerned with what is right, **yi** (義) (4.16).

Good government, for Kongzi, flows from good character rather than from clever laws. In a famous passage (2.3) he contrasts two methods. Guide people with regulations and keep them in line with punishments, and they will avoid trouble but have no sense of shame. Guide them with **de** (德), virtue or moral charisma, and keep them in line with li, and they will have a sense of shame and also order themselves. Compare Weber's types of authority from the Political track: Kongzi is betting on a kind of moral charisma made stable by ritual.

A related idea is **zhengming** (正名), 'rectifying names' (13.3). When names do not match realities, speech becomes confused, affairs fail, and punishments go astray. Asked about government, Kongzi said: let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son (12.11). This is not just about vocabulary. A 'father' who neglects his children, or a 'ruler' who plunders the people, does not deserve the name, and calling him by it disguises the failure. Later, Mencius would draw a bold conclusion: a tyrant who destroys ren and yi is a mere 'fellow', so killing him is not the murder of a ruler (Mencius 1B8).

sections.heading: Filial Piety and the Ethics of Roles
sections.body:
**Xiao** (孝), filial piety, is the root of Confucian ethics. The family is where we first learn to care, defer, remember and give. A disciple in the *Analects* calls filial and fraternal duty the root of ren (1.2).

Xiao is not mere obedience or material support. Kongzi complained (2.7) that people think filial piety means feeding their parents, but dogs and horses are fed too; without reverence, what is the difference? Children may disagree with parents, but should remonstrate gently, and if not heeded, remain respectful (4.18).

Here the hard cases begin. In *Analects* 13.18, a local lord boasts that in his region people are so upright that when a father steals a sheep, the son testifies against him. Kongzi replies that in his region uprightness is different: fathers cover for sons and sons cover for fathers, and uprightness lies in this. Mencius (7A35) imagines an even sharper dilemma: if the father of the sage-king Shun committed murder, Shun should not obstruct the judge, but he should give up his throne 'like an old sandal', carry his father on his back to the seashore, and live there happily, forgetting the empire.

These passages are not lazy nepotism. They express a considered view that special relationships are not just one value among many to be weighed impartially; they are part of what makes us moral beings at all. A person who would hand over their father without a moment's anguish might be impartial, but something has gone wrong with their humanity. Recall the ethics of care on Day 85: Nel Noddings and others also argue that morality grows from concrete relationships rather than abstract principles.

Some scholars, notably Roger Ames and Henry Rosemont, argue that Confucian thought is best understood not as a virtue ethics like Aristotle's (Day 20) but as **role ethics**: we are constituted by our roles (child, sibling, friend, teacher), and morality is the art of living those roles well. Others, such as Bryan Van Norden and Edward Slingerland, think the virtue ethics comparison is illuminating. This disagreement is itself a lesson in the risk of forcing one tradition into another's categories.

sections.heading: Mencius versus Xunzi: Is Human Nature Good?
sections.body:
Kongzi said little about **xing** (性), human nature. His followers fought about it for centuries.

**Mencius** (Mengzi, c. 372–289 BCE) held that human nature is good. His most famous argument is a thought experiment (2A6). Anyone who suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well will feel alarm and compassion, not because they want to win favour with the parents or praise from neighbours, or because they dislike the child's cries, but immediately. From such reactions Mencius concluded that every person has **four sprouts** (*siduan*): the feeling of compassion is the sprout of ren; shame and disdain, the sprout of yi; deference, the sprout of li; and the sense of approving and disapproving, the sprout of **zhi** (智), wisdom.

Sprouts are not full plants. They must be cultivated, and they can be stunted. In the parable of **Ox Mountain** (6A8), a once-lush mountain is bare because it was logged and grazed; people who see it think baldness is its nature. So too, people who seem wicked have had their sprouts cut down by bad circumstances. But cultivation must not be forced: Mencius mocks a farmer from Song who, worried his crops were slow, pulled on the shoots to help them grow, and killed them (2A2).

**Xunzi** (c. 310–c. 235 BCE), the most systematic early Confucian, answered bluntly: human nature is bad, and goodness is the product of deliberate effort, **wei** (偽) (chapter 23). Left to ourselves we are born with desires for profit, envy and hatred, and following them leads to strife. Goodness is like a straight board: wood must be steamed and pressed against a straightening frame. The sage-kings, seeing the chaos of unregulated desire, created li and yi to shape and satisfy desires in orderly ways (chapter 19).

Notice that both are Confucians. Both prize learning, ritual and the sages. They disagree about whether ritual *develops* something already in us (Mencius) or *imposes* something we lack (Xunzi). Who has the better evidence? Mencius can point to spontaneous empathy; Xunzi can point out that the child-at-the-well feeling is fleeting and easily overridden. Modern developmental psychology gives each something: infants show early prosocial tendencies, and also strong in-group bias and possessiveness. Strikingly, Xunzi's pupils included Han Feizi and Li Si, architects of the harsh Legalist state of Qin, though Xunzi himself never abandoned the priority of ritual and virtue over punishment.

sections.heading: Legacy and Critique
sections.body:
After the brutal Qin dynasty fell, the Han dynasty adopted Confucianism as state orthodoxy (from the reign of Emperor Wu, second century BCE). For roughly two thousand years, mastery of the Confucian classics was the route to government office through the imperial examination system, abolished only in 1905. In the Song dynasty, **Zhu Xi** (1130–1200) built a vast **Neo-Confucian** synthesis, partly in response to Buddhism, that placed Mencius's view of good human nature at its centre. Confucian ideas spread throughout Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

The tradition has faced fierce criticism, much of it from within East Asia. Its earliest rivals, the **Mohists** led by Mozi (5th century BCE), attacked it for partiality: why should I love my own family more than others' families? They urged impartial care (*jian ai*) and ridiculed lavish funerals as waste. In the twentieth century, Chinese reformers of the May Fourth Movement (1919) blamed Confucian hierarchy for stifling individuality, science and women's freedom. The classical texts do assume gendered roles, and the later 'three bonds' (ruler over minister, father over son, husband over wife) became instruments of domination.

Defenders reply that hierarchy in the classical texts is supposed to be reciprocal: the ruler must be ruler-like, and the father father-like, for the deference to be owed. Contemporary scholars such as Joseph Chan explore whether a 'Confucian perfectionism' can be combined with democracy and human rights, while others, like Sor-hoon Tan and Chenyang Li, develop Confucian feminism or Confucian democracy. The live question is whether the core insights (that character is formed through practice, that relationships are central to the good life, that rituals carry moral meaning) can be separated from the historical hierarchies they once supported.

keyQuote.text: What you do not want for yourself, do not do to others.
keyQuote.source: Confucius, Analects 15.24 (Kongzi's explanation of shu, reciprocity)

modernConnection.title: Rituals, Habits and the Law of Visiting Your Parents
modernConnection.body:
Confucian ideas are back in surprising places. Psychologists studying habit formation report that behaviour repeated in stable contexts becomes automatic, demanding less willpower. Kongzi would not be surprised. His claim was that character is built by practising forms until they feel natural, the way he describes himself at seventy, following his desires without overstepping. Organisations increasingly design small rituals on purpose: team check-ins, gratitude rounds, onboarding ceremonies, structured ways to disagree. Research on rituals, including studies by Michael Norton and Francesca Gino, suggests that even arbitrary ritual actions can reduce anxiety and grief. At Harvard, Michael Puett's popular course on Chinese philosophy (later the book *The Path*, 2016, with Christine Gross-Loh) pitched Confucian li as practical training in noticing and responding to others.

Filial piety has also returned to law. China's amended Law on the Protection of the Rights and Interests of the Elderly (in force from 2013) states that family members living apart from elderly relatives should visit or keep in touch with them often. Singapore's Maintenance of Parents Act (1995) allows elderly parents to claim financial support from their adult children. With ageing populations across East Asia and Europe, the question of what children owe parents is no longer abstract.

Yet the comparison exposes a tension Kongzi himself identified. Analects 2.3 said that rule by law and punishment produces compliance without shame, while rule by virtue and ritual produces genuine transformation. A law requiring visits can secure the visit but not the reverence; a corporate ritual imposed cynically becomes the empty form Kongzi deplored. The Confucian lesson is not that rituals are good in themselves, but that well-chosen forms, performed sincerely, can train the heart. Whether any institution can engineer that sincerity is the open question. Xunzi would be more optimistic than Mencius here: he thought forms practised long enough reshape desire itself, so that people come to love what they were first made to do. Anyone who has kept up a habit of thanking a colleague, or of calling a parent every Sunday, can test which of the two was closer to the truth.

vocabulary.definition: Humaneness or benevolence; the complete virtue of being humanly good in relation to others.
vocabulary.example: Kongzi rarely granted that anyone had achieved ren, treating it as a lifelong aspiration.

vocabulary.definition: Ritual propriety; the shared forms of conduct, from sacrifices to everyday courtesies, that structure social life.
vocabulary.example: For Fingarette, a handshake is a small instance of li that achieves recognition effortlessly.

vocabulary.definition: The exemplary person; originally 'son of a lord', redefined by Kongzi as a person of cultivated character regardless of birth.
vocabulary.example: The junzi asks what is right, while the small person asks what is profitable.

vocabulary.definition: Filial piety; reverent care and respect for parents and ancestors, seen as the root of other virtues.
vocabulary.example: Kongzi insisted that xiao requires reverence, not merely feeding one's parents.

vocabulary.definition: Rectifying names; making titles and roles match the conduct they imply.
vocabulary.example: Mencius used zhengming to argue that a tyrant forfeits the name of 'ruler'.

vocabulary.definition: Mencius's term for innate beginnings of compassion, shame, deference and moral discernment, which grow into ren, yi, li and zhi.
vocabulary.example: The alarm anyone feels at a child near a well reveals the sprout of compassion.

vocabulary.definition: In Xunzi, deliberate effort or artifice; the conscious cultivation by which goodness is produced from an unruly nature.
vocabulary.example: For Xunzi, a good person is like a straightened board, the product of wei rather than raw nature.

vocabulary.definition: The interpretation of Confucianism (associated with Ames and Rosemont) on which persons are constituted by their relationships and morality is excellence in fulfilling roles.
vocabulary.example: On a role ethics reading, asking what you owe 'as a human being' in the abstract is the wrong question.

thinkingExercise.title: Auditing Your Rituals
thinkingExercise.prompt: Look closely at the rituals already in your life, from greetings to meals to holidays, and ask what they are doing to your character and your relationships.
steps: List five small rituals you perform regularly (how you greet colleagues, a family meal, a text you always send, a way of saying goodbye).
For each, ask Kongzi's question: is it performed with ren (genuine care) or has it become empty form? What would make it sincere again?
Pick one relationship (a parent, sibling or close friend) and describe what xiao or its equivalent would require of you, beyond material help.

Decide between Mencius and Xunzi on the basis of your own experience: when you have become better, did it feel like growth of something already there or like reshaping something resistant? Give an example.

summary: Kongzi located morality in relationships and shared forms; the Analects is a layered collection of his sayings compiled by later disciples.
Ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety) are mutually dependent: form without care is empty, care without form is clumsy.
The junzi is an aristocrat of character; good government works through virtue and ritual rather than punishment, and names must match realities.
Filial piety roots ethics in the family, producing hard cases (the sheep-stealing father) that challenge impartial morality.
Mencius held human nature good (the four sprouts); Xunzi held it bad and goodness the product of deliberate effort; both prized ritual and learning.
Critics from the Mohists to the May Fourth reformers attacked partiality and hierarchy; contemporary Confucians debate whether its core can be democratic and egalitarian.

quiz.question: According to the lesson, what is the best description of the relationship between ren and li?
options: Ren is a legal code and li a feeling
They are mutually dependent: ritual is the form, humaneness the spirit
Li replaced ren in Kongzi's later thought
They are two names for the same rule of reciprocity
quiz.explanation: Kongzi links restraint and return to li with ren, but also says li means nothing without ren; each needs the other.

quiz.question: Fingarette's handshake example is meant to show that:
options: Confucian ritual is merely superstitious magic
Shared ceremonial forms accomplish real social effects effortlessly
Western etiquette is superior to Chinese ritual
Rituals should be replaced by explicit contracts
quiz.explanation: The handshake accomplishes mutual recognition without calculation; Fingarette calls this the 'magic' of li.

quiz.question: How did Kongzi transform the term junzi?
options: From 'exemplary person' into 'soldier'
From 'ruler' into 'minister'
From a title of noble birth into an ideal of cultivated character open to anyone
From a religious title into a legal office
quiz.explanation: Junzi once meant 'son of a lord'; Kongzi made it an ideal achieved by learning and self-cultivation.

quiz.question: In Analects 2.3, Kongzi argues that laws and punishments produce people who avoid trouble but lack a sense of shame.
quiz.explanation: He contrasts rule by regulation and punishment with rule by virtue and ritual, which produces shame and self-ordering.

quiz.question: Which story does Mencius use to argue that human nature contains a sprout of compassion?
options: The farmer of Song pulling on his crops
Ox Mountain's bare slopes
A child about to fall into a well
Shun carrying his father to the seashore
quiz.explanation: The immediate alarm anyone feels at a child near a well shows, for Mencius, an innate sprout of compassion.

quiz.question: Xunzi's image of steaming and straightening wood illustrates his view that:
options: Goodness comes from deliberate effort reshaping an unruly nature
Human nature is naturally straight and only needs protection
Rituals are useless restrictions
Only the emperor can become good
quiz.explanation: For Xunzi goodness is a product of wei, artifice, like wood bent straight against a frame.

quiz.question: Mencius and Xunzi disagreed about whether ritual and learning matter for becoming good.
quiz.explanation: Both prized ritual and learning; they disagreed about human nature, and so about whether ritual develops or imposes goodness.

quiz.question: A judge must decide whether to excuse a witness from testifying against her own father. Which Confucian text most directly addresses this situation?
options: Analects 13.18, on the son and the stolen sheep
Xunzi chapter 19, on the origin of ritual
Analects 2.4, on stages of life
Mencius 2A2, on pulling sprouts
quiz.explanation: In 13.18 Kongzi says fathers and sons cover for each other, prioritising family bonds over impartial testimony.

quiz.question: The Mohists' main criticism of Confucian ethics was that it was:
options: Too individualistic
Too focused on profit
Atheistic
Partial, favouring one's own family, and wasteful in ritual
quiz.explanation: Mozi urged impartial care (jian ai) and attacked lavish funerals, criticising Confucian partiality toward kin. Confucians, not Mohists, were the ones warning against profit-seeking.

quiz.question: Scholars agree that Confucian ethics is simply a Chinese version of Aristotle's virtue ethics.
quiz.explanation: Ames and Rosemont argue for 'role ethics' instead, while Van Norden and Slingerland find the virtue comparison illuminating; it is a live debate.

goDeeper.body:
One of the richest modern debates concerns **moral psychology**: how exactly does ritual practice change a person? Edward Slingerland's *Trying Not to Try* (2014) connects early Chinese ideals of effortless virtue to cognitive science, arguing that both Confucians and Daoists faced the 'paradox of wu-wei': how can you try to become someone who acts well without trying? Mencius thinks you must nurture sprouts already present; Xunzi thinks you must submit for years to external forms until they become second nature. Slingerland suggests each strategy has costs: Mencius struggles to explain why the sprouts so often fail, and Xunzi struggles to explain why anyone would come to love the rituals rather than merely obey them.

A second debate concerns **Confucianism and democracy**. Some, like Daniel A. Bell, defend 'political meritocracy' inspired by Confucian ideals of rule by the virtuous and learned, and point to China's selection of officials as a partial example. Critics reply that meritocracy without accountability invites abuse, and that Mencius himself held that Heaven sees as the people see, which can be read as a proto-democratic check. Joseph Chan's *Confucian Perfectionism* (2014) takes a middle path, arguing that Confucian values can justify democratic institutions instrumentally while rejecting the liberal idea that the state must be neutral about the good life.

Finally, the comparison between Mencius's sprouts and Aristotle's habituation (Day 20) is a classic of comparative philosophy. Lee Yearley's *Mencius and Aquinas* (1990) remains a model of how to compare traditions without flattening them.

readings.title: Confucius: Analects
readings.author: Edward Slingerland (translator)
readings.note: Includes selections from traditional commentaries, which show how the terse sayings were read.

readings.title: Confucius: The Secular as Sacred
readings.author: Herbert Fingarette
readings.note: A short, provocative book; read the first chapter on ritual as 'magic'.

readings.title: Mengzi: With Selections from Traditional Commentaries
readings.author: Bryan W. Van Norden (translator)
readings.note: Read 2A6 (the child and the well), 6A8 (Ox Mountain) and the debates with Gaozi in Book 6A.

readings.title: Xunzi: The Complete Text
readings.author: Eric L. Hutton (translator)
readings.note: Chapter 23, 'Human Nature Is Bad', and chapter 19, 'Discourse on Ritual'.

questions: Is Kongzi's answer in the stolen sheep case a moral insight or a recipe for corruption? Could a modern legal system accommodate it?
If rituals shape character, who should choose which rituals a society practises?
Can a role-based ethics give strangers, foreigners or future generations the moral standing they deserve?
